## Mathematical foundations

The common mathematical substrate is a graph-coupled dynamical system.
With agents \(i=1,\dots,n\), states \(x_i\), controls \(u_i\), and communication graph \(G=(V,E)\), one writes \[ \dot{x}_i=f_i(x_i,u_i,w_i), \qquad L = D-A, \] where \(A\) is the adjacency matrix, \(D\) the degree matrix, and \(L\) the graph Laplacian.
Most swarm theorems are ultimately about how the properties of \(L\) and the switching graph determine agreement, robustness, and convergence speed.
The algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2(L)\) governs many convergence and robustness margins in undirected graphs, while directed and switching graphs require stronger rootedness or robustness assumptions. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn14search0

For average consensus, the canonical continuous-time law is \[ \dot{x}=-Lx, \] and the discrete-time form is \[ x_{k+1}=Wx_k,\qquad W\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1. \] On a connected undirected graph with disagreement vector \(y=(I-J)x\), \(J=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), one standard Lyapunov function \(V=\tfrac12\|y\|_2^2\) yields \[ \dot V=-y^\top Ly \le -\lambda_2(L)\|y\|_2^2 = -2\lambda_2(L)V, \] so \[ \|y(t)\|_2 \le e^{-\lambda_2(L)t}\|y(0)\|_2. \] This is the canonical example of a rate bound driven by spectral gap.
For randomized gossip, the same intuition appears in expectation via the second-largest eigenvalue of the averaging operator. citeturn25view0turn25view3

Formation control usually replaces agreement on a scalar or vector state by agreement on relative geometry.
A standard distance-based objective is \[ e_{ij}(p)=\|p_i-p_j\|^2-d_{ij}^2, \] with gradient control \[ u_i=-\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\nabla_{p_i}\phi(e_{ij}), \] where \(d_{ij}\) are desired distances and \(\phi\) is a potential.
Rigidity theory explains when the target shape is locally unique up to translations and rotations.
In practice, a rigid interaction graph gives local shape identifiability, while the Hessian of the potential near the target determines local stability properties. citeturn32search6turn32search2

Flocking laws add velocity alignment and collision-avoidance or cohesion terms.
In the spirit of Cucker–Smale or Olfati-Saber, \[ \dot p_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=\sum_{j}a_{ij}(t)(v_j-v_i)-\nabla_{p_i}U(p), \] where \(U(p)\) penalizes unsafe separations or shape deviations.
The main proof patterns use Lyapunov-like kinetic-plus-potential energies and connectivity conditions on \(a_{ij}\).
These models are useful because they make explicit the trade between alignment, cohesion, obstacle avoidance, and scalability. citeturn10search21turn25view0turn43search0

Distributed optimization enters when control is recast as minimizing a sum of local costs: \[ \min_{x_1,\dots,x_n} \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x_i=z. \] A standard consensus-ADMM iteration is \[ x_i^{k+1}=\arg\min_{x_i}\Big(f_i(x_i)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x_i-z^k+u_i^k\|^2\Big), \] \[ z^{k+1}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i^{k+1}+u_i^k),\qquad u_i^{k+1}=u_i^k+x_i^{k+1}-z^{k+1}. \] ADMM is attractive because it separates local computation from network consensus, and for convex problems its ergodic convergence is often \(O(1/k)\), though real-time embedded performance is driven more by communication rounds and warm-start quality than asymptotic notation. citeturn25view4turn10search12

Game theory is increasingly relevant for contested or congested settings.
Small-team planning uses auction, contract-net, or Nash-equilibrium ideas; very large swarms use mean-field approximations in which the empirical distribution of agent states replaces pairwise coupling.
A generic mean-field objective is \[ J_i(u_i)=\mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^T \ell(x_i(t),u_i(t),m_t)\,dt + g(x_i(T),m_T)\right], \] where \(m_t\) is the swarm state distribution.
Mean-field models reduce all-pairs complexity and are mathematically natural for \(N\to\infty\), but they can underrepresent finite-team heterogeneity and local sensing constraints. citeturn11search13turn11search0

State estimation still relies on filtering.
For linear-Gaussian models, the Kalman recursion is \[ \hat x_{k|k-1}=A\hat x_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=AP_{k-1|k-1}A^\top+Q, \] \[ K_k=P_{k|k-1}H^\top(HP_{k|k-1}H^\top+R)^{-1}, \] \[ \hat x_{k|k}=\hat x_{k|k-1}+K_k(y_k-H\hat x_{k|k-1}). \] Distributed Kalman filtering adds either estimate-sharing or measurement-sharing plus a consensus stage.
The main technical difficulty is that communication constraints and correlated noise can make naive fusion inconsistent; this is why the distributed-estimation literature now pays explicit attention to communication budget, covariance consistency, and Bayesian lower bounds. citeturn10search14turn38search0turn38search9

## Learning and AI methods

Modern swarm learning is dominated by **centralized training with decentralized execution**.
The basic objective is still \[ J(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^t r_t\right], \] but the learning problem is harder than in single-agent RL because each agent’s environment becomes non-stationary when the other agents are learning at the same time.
This non-stationarity is explicit in the MADDPG paper, which also notes that policy-gradient variance rises with agent count. citeturn35view5

For actor–critic methods, MADDPG uses a centralized critic and decentralized actors: \[ \nabla_{\theta_i}J \approx \mathbb E\!\left[\nabla_{\theta_i}\pi_i(o_i)\,\nabla_{a_i}Q_i(x,a_1,\dots,a_n)\right]. \] The advantage is coordination under mixed cooperative–competitive settings; the drawback is poor scaling when the critic must condition on large joint observation–action spaces.
In practice, this is why locality restrictions, factorization, graph neural policies, or parameter sharing are often introduced for larger swarms. citeturn35view5turn28search12

Value-factorization methods trade expressivity for tractability.
QMIX constructs a joint action-value \(Q_{\text{tot}}\) as a monotonic combination of per-agent values \(Q_a\), subject to \[ \frac{\partial Q_{\text{tot}}}{\partial Q_a}\ge 0. \] This guarantees that decentralized greedy action selection is consistent with maximizing the centralized value, which is powerful for cooperative tasks but restrictive if true coordination requires non-monotone interactions. citeturn35view6turn28search17

On-policy PPO-style methods have become much more important than older MARL folk wisdom predicted.
MAPPO showed strong performance on particle-world, SMAC, Google Research Football, and Hanabi with comparatively modest tuning, and HAPPO later added a stronger trust-region style theory with a monotonic-improvement result through sequential policy updates and a multi-agent advantage decomposition.
The consequence is that the practical frontier is no longer “off-policy only”; for many cooperative multi-UAV planning problems, PPO-family methods are credible first baselines. citeturn36view0turn35view8

Imitation learning remains highly relevant for flight.
Behavior cloning is simple and cheap but brittle under compounding distribution shift; DAgger addresses this by iteratively aggregating expert labels on states visited by the learner.
For aerial robotics, this is still one of the most practical routes to high-level navigation skills when demonstrations are available but online exploratory RL is unsafe or too data-hungry. citeturn30search0turn30search2turn30search9

Federated and meta-learning are natural extensions for swarms.
FedAvg updates a shared model by weighted averaging, \[ w^{t+1}=\sum_i \frac{n_i}{\sum_j n_j}w_i^{t+1}, \] which preserves raw-data locality and reduces central data collection; MAML seeks an initialization \(\theta\) that adapts quickly via \[ \theta_i'=\theta-\alpha\nabla_\theta \mathcal L_{\tau_i}(\theta). \] In UAV networks, these paradigms are attractive because observations are distributed, links are constrained, and environments change quickly.
The main caveat is that non-IID data, unstable topology, and energy limits can destroy the idealized communication assumptions of standard FL and meta-learning. citeturn37search0turn37search3turn37search1turn37search7turn37search2turn37search8

Model-based and model-free learning should not be framed as a winner-take-all dichotomy.
PETS and MBPO showed why learned dynamics models can drastically improve sample efficiency or even support monotonic-improvement analyses, but these methods remain vulnerable to model bias outside the training envelope.
Model-free systems remain attractive for expressive policies in poorly modeled settings, especially when high-fidelity simulators or offline logs exist.
In practice, the most successful autonomy stacks increasingly use model-based planning or safety filtering around learned perception and policy modules. citeturn31search0turn31search1turn31search5turn31search18

The strongest recent safety-learning line in multi-agent control uses control barrier functions.
The CBF condition \[ \dot h(x,u)+\alpha(h(x))\ge 0 \] defines a forward-invariant safe set \(\{x:h(x)\ge 0\}\) under suitable regularity assumptions.
Learning-based approaches now jointly learn decentralized CBFs and policies, and GCBF+ extends this line with graph neural parameterizations and LiDAR point clouds, including hardware demonstrations on drone swarms.
This is one of the clearest examples of a method that is genuinely both “AI” and “certifiable” in a swarm-relevant sense. citeturn35view3turn28search7turn28search19

A still-emerging layer is the use of large language or multimodal foundation models at the task-planning and human-swarm interface level.
Current survey evidence suggests value for natural-language tasking, multimodal scene interpretation, and collaborative mission management, but not yet a replacement for low-level verified control.
In safety-critical air operations, the most defensible architecture is hierarchical: language model for intent and decomposition, optimization/control for trajectory generation, and certified safety shields for execution. citeturn29search14turn35view2turn35view0

## Communication, hardware, and systems architecture

Communication is not a support function in swarms; it is part of the control plant.
The most important co-design question is whether state exchange should be periodic, event-triggered, summarized, or omitted altogether.
ROS 2 documentation makes the core trade explicit: DDS/ROS 2 can be tuned between “best effort” and “reliable,” with incompatible QoS profiles causing message loss by construction.
In lossy wireless environments, best-effort often reduces traffic and recovery overhead, while reliable delivery can become pathological when IP fragmentation fills buffers and stalls traffic.
This is exactly why communication-aware consensus and event-triggered control remain mathematically and operationally important. citeturn26view3turn26view2turn25view9turn26view1

The communications menu spans low-power local links, mesh-style tactical links, broadband local WLAN, and cellular connectivity.
The raw data-rate spread is enormous: LoRaWAN regional data rates can range from hundreds of bit/s to tens of kbit/s depending on scheme and region; IEEE 802.15.4 targets 250 kbit/s; Bluetooth LE supports 1 Mb/s and optional 2 Mb/s or coded 125/500 kb/s modes; Wi‑Fi 6 advertises a theoretical 9.6 Gb/s aggregate maximum; and 3rd Generation Partnership Project states that its first 5G NR UAV release provides the foundation for connecting drones over cellular networks, though UAV-specific public throughput figures are not specified on the cited page.
These rates are not operationally comparable one-for-one because topology, duty cycle, contention, and link budget are different, but the order-of-magnitude differences matter for architecture design. citeturn39view3turn39view4turn39view2turn39view1turn39view0

The dominant open software pattern is a split architecture: a real-time flight stack on the flight controller, plus a more capable companion computer for perception, planning, or coordination.
PX4 explicitly separates a flight stack from middleware and treats the overall system as asynchronous message-passing modules; its uXRCE-DDS bridge exposes uORB topics to ROS 2 via a client–agent architecture over serial or UDP.
ArduPilot uses a similar companion-computer pattern over MAVLink. micro-ROS and Micro XRCE-DDS are attractive on very resource-constrained nodes because the client side is designed for low memory footprints and flexible transports. citeturn27view0turn27view1turn27view3turn27view4

It is a synthesis from PX4, ROS 2/DDS, MAVLink, ArduPilot, and digital-twin workflows. citeturn27view0turn27view1turn26view3turn27view2turn27view3turn12search19turn12search15

Energy is the other hard systems constraint.
A useful aggregate budget is \[ E_{\text{avail}} \ge \int_0^T \left(P_{\text{prop}}+P_{\text{compute}}+P_{\text{payload}}+P_{\text{comm}}\right)\,dt. \] For multirotors, propulsion dominates most missions, so additional onboard AI or communications are usually secondary but still non-negligible for small airframes.
The important engineering consequence is that sensing, compute, and communication cannot be scaled independently of airframe size, rotor disk area, payload mass, and thermal limits. citeturn24search0turn24search4turn24search7

On sensing, the robust minimum set for serious autonomy is still IMU + GNSS + barometer + magnetometer, typically augmented by camera, depth, or LiDAR, and increasingly thermal or radar in specialized missions.
Vision-inertial systems such as VINS-Fusion and related deployments remain central because they offer accurate localization for autonomous drones and even cooperating UAV teams where GNSS is degraded.
The open problem is not whether good estimators exist; it is whether they remain calibrated and certifiable under the full range of lighting, weather, texture, motion blur, and adversarial disturbances seen in real operations. citeturn38search8turn38search11turn27view3

## Verification, security, resilience, and testing

Simulation is the first assurance layer.
Gazebo provides high-fidelity physics, rendering, and sensor models; PX4 and ArduPilot both support software-in-the-loop and multi-vehicle scenarios with Gazebo; AirSim targets physically and visually realistic simulation with flight-controller integration; and FlightGoggles adds photorealistic sensor rendering and powerful vehicle-in-the-loop support.
These tools are mature enough for perception and controller development, but none on its own solves the joint problem of aerodynamics, communications, digital infrastructure, and regulation-aware traffic interaction. citeturn13search2turn13search6turn13search13turn13search0turn13search11turn13search1

That gap is why digital twins are becoming important.
Recent work argues for coupling vehicle physics, communications emulation, and telemetry analytics, and systems such as GazeboNS3 explicitly target the missing bridge between physical drone simulation and network experimentation.
For swarms, this is not a luxury: verification that ignores the network is verifying the wrong system. citeturn12search15turn12search19turn12search7

Formal methods are the second assurance layer.
Hamilton–Jacobi reachability computes backward- or forward-reachable safe sets by solving a dynamic-programming PDE of the form \[ \partial_t V(x,t)+\min_u\max_d \nabla V(x,t)^\top f(x,u,d)=0, \] with the zero sublevel set encoding safety or goal reachability.
Its advantage is rigorous guarantees under disturbances and adversaries; its disadvantage is dimensionality.
Recent work combining decomposition, warm starts, and adaptive grids showed one- to two-order-of-magnitude speedups and demonstrated updates for 10D near-hover quadcopters, which is materially important for aerial robotics. citeturn12search1turn35view2

Neural-network verification is now a serious, though still incomplete, complement.
NNV provides exact and over-approximate reachability for many network classes and learning-enabled CPS, including neural-network control systems.
This matters because more autonomy stacks now include small neural modules inside feedback loops, and empirical test coverage alone is insufficient for safety claims.
The current boundary is scalability: verification remains strongest for bounded architectures and simplified plant models, not for end-to-end large multimodal autonomy stacks. citeturn35view0turn35view1

Security and resilience start with consensus and estimation under attack.
Connectivity is not enough; resilient consensus requires graph robustness and local adversary-tolerant update rules such as W‑MSR-type filtering.
Byzantine-resilient optimization extends the same logic to distributed cost minimization, where even a single adversarial cost function can dominate a naive average.
Secure state estimation adds another line of defense when sensors or actuators may be corrupted. citeturn25view6turn25view7turn10search11turn10search3

For drones specifically, GNSS spoofing remains a serious threat surface, and anti-spoofing work such as SemperFi shows why receiver-level recovery and mitigation are necessary rather than simple anomaly detection alone.
However, navigation resilience should not be reduced to “GPS hardening.” The stronger approach is sensor diversity, estimator consistency checks, map- or vision-relative localization, trustworthy time synchronization, and mission modes that degrade gracefully when absolute positioning collapses. citeturn14search12turn14search5turn38search8turn38search11

Cyber-resilience in deployed fleets is increasingly informed by National Institute of Standards and Technology guidance and zero-trust principles.
CSF 2.0 provides a high-level cybersecurity outcomes taxonomy, and SP 800-207 frames zero trust as protection focused on users, assets, and resources rather than trusted network perimeters.
For drones, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency guidance emphasizes securing software and firmware, limiting exposed communications paths, and protecting data storage and transfer.
These are ordinary cyber controls, but in swarms they must be pushed down into airframe, radio, and mission-toolchain decisions. citeturn42view3turn42view4turn34search0turn15search19

Remote ID improves traceability but introduces new security and privacy questions.
FAA pages define it as broadcast identification and location information for in-flight drones, while recent research highlights privacy leakage and the need for stronger authentication because current broadcast ecosystems can be vulnerable to spoofing, relay, or replay.
The central design challenge is therefore dual: accountability to regulators and nearby airspace participants, but without unnecessarily exposing operators or creating unauthenticated trust in broadcast messages. citeturn42view0turn40academia9turn40academia10

What is still missing is a genuinely integrated assurance workflow.
The field has simulation tools, control proofs, neural verifiers, cyber frameworks, and test guidebooks, but the end-to-end pipeline from requirements to verified code to field telemetry to regression testing is still fragmented.
This is especially visible in defense documents that now explicitly call for iterative cyber T&E, realistic operational testing, and follow-on evaluation when system states or autonomy logic change. citeturn18view2turn19search2turn19search13

## Civic and defense contexts, regulation, ethics, and societal impacts

In civic settings, the most mature swarm-adjacent use cases are public safety, infrastructure inspection, mapping, communication relay, environmental monitoring, and delivery in managed corridors.
NIST’s public-safety UAS program frames the value proposition clearly: first responders use UAS for situational awareness in dangerous environments and often in degraded communications conditions; the same sources emphasize reliable communications, cybersecurity, and AI risk management rather than autonomy in the abstract.
The FAA BVLOS NPRM similarly lists package delivery, agriculture, aerial surveying, civic-interest uses, training, recreation, and flight testing as central integration targets. citeturn33view6turn33view5turn17view0turn18view0

Civil regulation is converging on three pillars.
The first is performance-based flight authorization for routine BVLOS and scalable UTM-like services.
The second is remote identification and operator traceability.
The third is structured airspace information and authorization services.
FAA Remote ID requires most registered drones to comply and offers three compliance pathways: standard Remote ID drones, Remote ID broadcast modules, or operation inside a FRIA.
EASA’s U-space makes mandatory services central to operation in designated airspace, including authorization, traffic information, and weather support, with certified providers and secure interoperable protocols.
ICAO guidance continues to emphasize harmonized integration of remotely piloted systems into non-segregated airspace. citeturn42view0turn41search1turn42view1turn42view2turn16search17

These rules are technically consequential.
Once flight authorization, remote identification, and traffic information become built-in assumptions, autonomy design is no longer just onboard control plus a radio.
It becomes a socio-technical system touching identity, data governance, airspace services, human oversight, and incident response.
This is one reason purely research-stack swarms often fail to transfer directly into civic operations even when the core control algorithms work. citeturn42view0turn42view2turn33view5

Ethically, the largest civic concerns are privacy, surveillance, nuisance, labor displacement, and unequal risk distribution.
Remote ID and public-safety integration may improve accountability, but they can also expose operator location and create powerful surveillance infrastructures if poorly governed.
The best current design principle is proportionality: collect and expose only the information necessary for safety and accountability, authenticate what is broadcast, and separate safety monitoring from unnecessary mass retention or public tracking. citeturn33view5turn40academia9turn42view0

Defense contexts raise different but related issues.
Official public doctrine and policy emphasize interoperability, responsible use, experimentation, and scalable systems of systems rather than endorsing unconstrained autonomous engagement.
NATO’s autonomy and AI strategy documents explicitly ground autonomy in international law and responsible-use principles.
DoD Directive 3000.09 requires appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force, realistic operational testing, cyber survivability, legal review, and procedures to avoid unintended engagements or unauthorized interference.
Public DARPA programs such as OFFSET show the technical focus on large-team human-swarm teaming and interfaces, while public solicitations such as AMASS indicate interest in broader multi-domain adaptive swarms-of-swarms. citeturn33view3turn33view4turn17view1turn18view2turn33view2turn20search1

The high-level operational considerations for defense swarms are therefore clear even without discussing tactics.
They must function with contested communications, spectrum pressure, deceptive sensing, heterogeneous assets, and partial observability.
They must support mission command and decentralized execution when links to higher headquarters or cloud resources disappear.
They must also remain inspectable enough that commanders and lawyers can understand, test, and constrain what the system will do in bounded conditions. citeturn20search17turn17view1turn33view3

Legally, the public international debate is still active.
ICRC materials describe autonomous weapon systems as systems that select and apply force without human intervention after activation and argue for new rules that prohibit unacceptable systems and restrict others.
CCW Group of Governmental Experts sessions continued in 2025, showing that no universal treaty settlement has yet emerged.
NATO’s principles rest on lawfulness, accountability, explainability/traceability, reliability, governability, and bias mitigation.
In U.S. practice, DoD’s public policy requires legal review, law-of-war consistency, and senior-level approvals for relevant classes of systems. citeturn22search1turn22search13turn22search0turn33view4turn17view1

The deepest societal issue spanning both civic and defense use is not autonomy alone but **governed autonomy**.
A swarm that is mathematically stable but institutionally unaccountable is not a mature technology.
Conversely, strong governance without robust estimation, networking, and safety proofs will not keep systems reliable in complex airspace or adversarial conditions.
The field’s real frontier is therefore technical–legal integration: proving enough to justify deployment, instrumenting enough to enable audits, and limiting enough to preserve human responsibility. citeturn33view5turn42view0turn17view1turn33view4turn22search13

### Open questions and limitations

Public quantitative data are still sparse for very large heterogeneous swarms, communication-denied missions, aerodynamic interaction effects, authenticated Remote ID deployments, and defense-only platforms.
Public endurance and payload figures are often mission-dependent or unspecified, and many high-value defense performance parameters are not disclosed.
On the mathematical side, the hardest unsolved intersection is still this: learned, partially observed, communication-constrained, adversarial multi-agent control with certifiable guarantees and realistic airspace compliance. citeturn7search14turn20search1turn40academia10turn35view2turn35view0

## Organizational implications and recommended use

This report is intended for organizations evaluating, funding, procuring, governing, or deploying autonomous-agent and drone-swarm capabilities.
The main practical conclusion is that organizations should evaluate swarms as **layered socio-technical systems**, not as standalone AI models or standalone aircraft.
The decisive questions are whether the operational envelope is bounded, whether communications and localization failure modes are known, whether the system can degrade safely, whether human oversight is explicit, and whether the safety case is supported by simulation, formal analysis, cyber testing, and field telemetry.

| Organizational function | What to take from this report | Practical implication |
|---|---|---|
| Executive leadership | Drone-swarm autonomy is mature for bounded tasks, not unrestricted open-world autonomy. | Treat near-term opportunities as managed-envelope deployments rather than general-purpose autonomous fleets. |
| Engineering and product teams | The state of the art is layered: graph control, estimation, optimization, task allocation, learned perception/policy, and safety filters. | Build architectures that separate mission planning, local control, communications, safety shields, and logging rather than relying on one end-to-end model. |
| Safety, assurance, and compliance teams | Certification-oriented methods such as Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, CBFs, barrier certificates, neural verification, simulation, and test/evaluation workflows are increasingly central. | Require explicit safety cases, safe-set definitions, degraded-mode behavior, and evidence from simulation plus field testing. |
| Cybersecurity teams | Swarms expand the attack surface across GNSS, firmware, radios, middleware, telemetry, Remote ID, and mission planning tools. | Apply zero-trust assumptions, authenticated communications where possible, sensor-diverse navigation, and adversary-aware testing. |
| Legal and policy teams | Civil and defense governance are moving toward BVLOS integration, Remote ID, U-space/UTM services, responsible AI, and explicit human judgment. | Tie procurement and deployment decisions to jurisdiction-specific aviation rules, privacy obligations, human-oversight requirements, and international humanitarian-law review where relevant. |
| Research and strategy teams | Open problems remain in learned, partially observed, communication-constrained, adversarial multi-agent control with certifiable guarantees. | Prioritize experiments that stress communications loss, sensor spoofing, heterogeneous teams, airspace integration, and auditability. |

For internal distribution, the report can be used as a common vocabulary document, a procurement-readiness checklist, a technical due-diligence frame, or a foundation for a more specialized roadmap.
It should not be treated as a deployment authorization.
Any organization moving toward field operations should supplement it with jurisdiction-specific legal review, airspace authorization analysis, site-specific safety assessment, spectrum planning, cybersecurity review, and operational test data.

The predicated analogue of the swarm-intelligence theorem [llm-swarms-fail-classical-conditions](../../../../../artificial-intelligence/theories/swarm-intelligence/theorems/llm-swarms-fail-classical-conditions.md).
Whereas LLM collectives fail the classical stigmergy convergence conditions because they violate *local determinism*, predicated drone collectives fail the classical conditions because they violate **symmetric handedness**: drones are receive-mostly with periodic state-broadcast, sensor reads are partial-observability, and physical actuation is precondition-bounded — none of these meet the classical stigmergy assumption that all participants exchange comparable signals symmetrically.

## Statement

**Theorem.** *Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a predicated drone collective: a finite set of embodied participants $\{d_1, \ldots, d_n\}$ with [embodied-handedness](teaching/explanations/embodied-handedness.md) coordinates $h(d_i) = (\mathrm{recv}_i, \mathrm{send}_i, \mathrm{actuate}_i, \mathrm{observe}_i)$.
Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the classical-stigmergy convergence conditions (uniform reciprocal signal exchange, symmetric local-state observation, time-invariant interaction graph).
Then:*

1. *(Asymmetry.)
  For embodied participants with $h(d_i) \neq h(d_j)$ for some $i, j$, the collective $\mathcal{D}$ fails $\mathcal{S}$ — specifically, fails the uniform-reciprocal-signal-exchange condition, since $d_i$'s send-handedness and $d_j$'s receive-handedness are unequal in general.*

2. *(Substrate compatibility despite failure.)
  Although $\mathcal{D}$ fails classical stigmergy, the substrate-side cell-update sub-layer satisfies the structural-stigmergy version per [stigmergy-as-substrate-feedback-channel](../../../../../../../../../tools/platform/pyfars/questions/stigmergy-decouples-coordination-cost.md): cell-merge under the substrate's bilattice valuation is a stigmergic-update step that converges to fixed point under closure-2-monad lax-idempotence regardless of the embodied participants' handedness asymmetry.*

3. *(Layered control implication.)
  The asymmetry-induced failure of classical stigmergy at the embodied layer requires a substrate-side coordination layer to mediate.
  This is the substrate-as-supervisor-of-layered-control commitment — PyFARS's three-layer architecture is the substrate-algebraic answer to this failure.*

## Why this matters

Classical multi-agent control theorems (consensus, formation, flocking) depend on stigmergy-style assumptions.
A drone collective that fails classical stigmergy cannot rely on those theorems' guarantees directly.
The theorem establishes that predicated drone collectives need the substrate-coordination layer; without it, embodied participants drift apart under handedness asymmetry alone.

## Proof sketch

Direct from the [`embodied-handedness`](teaching/explanations/embodied-handedness.md) concept's definition: handedness is a four-tuple $(\mathrm{recv}, \mathrm{send}, \mathrm{actuate}, \mathrm{observe})$ where each coordinate is a participant-specific bandwidth/rate/access predicate.
The classical-stigmergy uniform-reciprocal-exchange condition requires $\mathrm{recv}_i = \mathrm{send}_j$ for all $(i, j)$ pairs and $\mathrm{actuate}_i$ symmetric across participants.
Drones with heterogeneous airframes, sensors, and bandwidth budgets fail this; the failure is structural, not a tuning issue.

Part (2) follows from the [closure 2-monad lax-idempotence](../../../../../../../../../humanities/theories/math/theories/categories/theories/predication-categories/theorems/closure-2-monad-lax-idempotence.md) — the substrate's cell-update converges regardless of which participant emitted the update.

Part (3) is the engineering consequence: the substrate-coordination layer carries what classical stigmergy would have provided, and is the necessary structural element for an embodied-collective polity. ∎-sketch

## Position

Foundational regime classification for the sub-theory.
The theorem establishes that drone collectives require substrate-mediated coordination, which justifies the existence of the three-layer architecture and the [meaningful-human-control](meaningful-human-control-as-charter-c3-extension.md) charter-tier discipline as substrate-resident features.

## Open

- Quantitative bound on how much handedness asymmetry the substrate-coordination layer can absorb before scaling breaks.
  Conjectured: bounded by the [coordination-across-handedness theorem](coordination-across-handedness-asymmetric-participants.md)'s cohomology bound.
- Whether the failure of classical stigmergy implies failure of *all* classical convergence guarantees, or only the stigmergy-dependent ones.
  Likely the latter; consensus-on-graphs (with unequal weights) still applies under a weaker class of assumptions.

# From classical to LLM swarms: a history and a critique

The contemporary use of "swarm" in the LLM-agent literature carries implications inherited from a sixty-year intellectual history of swarm-intelligence research.
This narrative traces that history, the properties of the systems it studied, and the structural reasons that LLM-agent systems do not inherit those properties despite frequently being described in the same vocabulary.

## The biological roots: Grassé and the discovery of stigmergy (1959)

Pierre-Paul Grassé observed termites constructing elaborate nests without any individual termite holding a plan.
He coined the term *stigmergy* — from the Greek *stigma* (sign) and *ergon* (work) — to describe the coordination mechanism: each termite responds only to the local state of the partially constructed nest; the nest itself carries the coordination signal.
Subsequent biological work (E.O. Wilson on ants, work on social insects generally) established that stigmergic coordination is the dominant mechanism in social-insect societies and that the colony-level intelligence vastly exceeds what any individual insect could achieve.

The defining feature of stigmergic coordination, identified in this biological work, is *the decoupling of agents in space and time*: agents that never coexist still coordinate through their shared modifications to a persistent medium.
This is structurally different from any system in which agents communicate by direct messaging, and it is the property that the [stigmergy](../teaching/explanations/stigmergy.md) concept names.

## Reynolds and emergence: the boids model (1987)

Craig Reynolds' 1987 paper "Flocks, Herds and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model" demonstrated that complex flocking behavior emerges from three simple local rules — separation, alignment, and cohesion — applied identically by every simulated bird (boid).
No boid contained a representation of "the flock"; the flock-level behavior was an *emergent* property of the local rules.

Reynolds' contribution was methodological: it established that emergence is a constructive property of well-chosen local rules, not a mysterious systems property.
The [emergence](../teaching/explanations/emergence.md) concept and the [emergence-requires-local-determinism](../theorems/emergence-requires-local-determinism.md) theorem are direct intellectual descendants of this constructive view.

## Dorigo and Ant Colony Optimization (1992)

Marco Dorigo's 1992 PhD thesis introduced Ant Colony Optimization, translating the biological pheromone-trail mechanism into a combinatorial-optimization algorithm.
The key technical contributions: the [pheromone field](../objects/pheromone-field.md) abstraction with explicit deposition and evaporation operators, the probability sampling rule for path selection, and (in subsequent work with Stützle) the explicit boundedness conditions that yield the [aco-convergence](../theorems/aco-convergence.md) theorem.

ACO became the canonical demonstration that swarm-intelligence ideas could deliver competitive performance on hard combinatorial-optimization problems (TSP, vehicle routing, network routing, scheduling).
It established that "swarm intelligence" is not just biological description but a genuine engineering paradigm.

## Kennedy and Eberhart and Particle Swarm Optimization (1995)

James Kennedy and Russell Eberhart's 1995 paper introduced Particle Swarm Optimization, motivated by Reynolds' boids and by social- psychological models of opinion dynamics.
Each particle moved in a search space, adjusting its velocity based on its own best-observed position and the swarm's best-observed position.
Subsequent analytical work (Clerc–Kennedy 2002; Trelea 2003) established the parameter regions for stable convergence, yielding the [pso-local-convergence](../theorems/pso-local-convergence.md) theorem.

PSO and ACO became the two canonical swarm-intelligence algorithms, each with formal convergence guarantees and broad practical adoption.

## The consolidating textbook: Bonabeau, Dorigo, Theraulaz (1999)

*Swarm Intelligence: From Natural to Artificial Systems* (1999) consolidated the field.
It established the standard taxonomy of mechanisms (stigmergy, self-organization, emergence), the canonical algorithms (ACO, PSO, and several others), and the structural properties that distinguish swarm-intelligence systems from other multi-agent systems: the [scalability premise](../teaching/explanations/scalability-premise.md), [homogeneity](../teaching/explanations/homogeneity.md), and the central role of [local-rule coordination](../teaching/explanations/local-rule-coordination.md).

The textbook also established the field's normative commitment: swarm intelligence is the study of *cheap, simple agents producing coordinated behavior at scale*.
The cost asymmetry — many cheap agents collectively outperforming few expensive ones — is the structural identity of the field.

## The arrival of LLM agents (2022–2024)

The arrival of LLM-based agentic systems in 2022–2024 was accompanied by an immediate vocabulary appropriation.
"Swarm" terminology was applied freely to multi-agent LLM systems: OpenAI's "Swarm" framework for handoff-based agent coordination, "AgentVerse," "AutoGen multi-agent debate," and many others.
The implicit suggestion: these systems inherited the desirable properties of classical swarm-intelligence systems.

By the analysis of the [swarm-vs-orchestration-dichotomy](../theorems/swarm-vs-orchestration-dichotomy.md) theorem, this is wrong: most "LLM swarm" architectures are orchestrated multi-agent systems in the precise sense of the [agents theory](../../agents/_index.md).
They do not satisfy the three swarm-coordinated conditions and do not inherit any of the classical swarm-intelligence convergence guarantees.

## The 2025 critique: Doan et al.

In June 2025, Doan et al.'s arXiv preprint *"LLM-Powered Swarms: A New Frontier or a Conceptual Stretch?"* (arXiv 2506.14496) made the critique explicit.
The paper's central argument:

- LLM agents violate the **scalability premise** by many orders of magnitude.
- Natural-language coordination violates the **local-rule** discipline.
- Closed-form convergence guarantees do not transfer.

The paper does not deny that LLM-agent collectives can be useful; it denies that they are swarms in the technical sense the classical literature established.
The [llm-swarms-fail-classical-conditions](../theorems/llm-swarms-fail-classical-conditions.md) theorem makes this critique precise within the present theory.

## Where this leaves us

The field is at an honest impasse.
There is no mathematical theory of LLM-agent collectives comparable in rigor to classical swarm- intelligence theory.
There are open research directions ([when-do-llm-agents-form-a-swarm](../learning/questions/when-do-llm-agents-form-a-swarm.md); [stigmergic-context-engineering](../learning/questions/stigmergic-context-engineering.md); [hybrid-swarm-orchestration](../learning/questions/hybrid-swarm-orchestration.md)) that may close the gap, but as of mid-2026 they have not.

The honest engineering position is:

- Use LLM-agent systems where their flexibility and reasoning power justify the cost; deploy them as orchestrated systems with the cost properties characterized by the [agents](../../agents/_index.md) theory.
- Use classical swarm-intelligence algorithms where the problem fits: combinatorial optimization, function optimization, pattern formation, routing.
- Do not expect a single architecture to deliver both the reasoning power of LLMs and the cost properties of classical swarms.
  The swarm-vs-orchestration dichotomy is structural.

# ACO convergence

**Claim.** Ant Colony Optimization with bounded pheromone updates, positive pheromone evaporation, lower bound $\tau_{\min} > 0$ on pheromone values, and an elitist archive (best-so-far solution preservation) converges to the global optimum of a finite combinatorial optimization problem with probability one as the number of iterations goes to infinity.

This is the canonical convergence result for stigmergic swarm algorithms.
The proof is due to Stützle & Hoos (2000) for the MAX-MIN Ant System variant and is recapitulated in Dorigo & Stützle (2004), *Ant Colony Optimization*.

## Statement

Let $S$ be the finite set of solutions to a combinatorial optimization problem with objective $f : S \to \mathbb{R}$.
Let $s^* \in \arg\max_{s \in S} f(s)$ be a global optimum.
Run an ACO algorithm with:

- Pheromone field $\tau_t : E \to [\tau_{\min}, \tau_{\max}]$ on the problem's solution-component edges $E$, with $0 < \tau_{\min} < \tau_{\max} < \infty$;
- Bounded deposition: $\Delta\tau^{(i)}_t \leq \Delta\tau_{\max}$ for all agents $i$ and times $t$;
- Positive evaporation: $\rho \in (0, 1)$;
- Elitist archive: the best-so-far solution $s^{\text{best}}_t$ is retained across iterations and contributes to deposition at every iteration.

Then:

$$ \Pr\left[ s^{\text{best}}_t = s^* \right] \to 1 \text{ as } t \to \infty $$

That is, the probability that the elitist archive contains the global optimum approaches one.

## Proof sketch

The proof has three steps:

**Step 1: every solution has positive probability at every iteration.** Because $\tau_t(e) \geq \tau_{\min} > 0$ for every edge $e$, the probability that any complete solution path is sampled by some ant in some iteration is bounded below by a positive constant $p_{\min}$ depending on $\tau_{\min}$ and the solution-space size.
By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma, the global optimum $s^*$ is sampled infinitely often with probability one.

**Step 2: the elitist archive is monotone.** When the elitist archive records the best-so-far, $f(s^{\text{best}}_{t+1}) \geq f(s^{\text{best}}_t)$ for every $t$, with equality unless a better solution was found.
Combined with Step 1, the archive eventually contains $s^*$ with probability one.

**Step 3: once $s^*$ is in the archive, it remains.** The elitist discipline keeps $s^*$ in the archive once recorded.

Combining: $\Pr[s^{\text{best}}_t = s^*] \to 1$.

## What the proof requires

The four hypotheses are all necessary:

- **Lower-bounded pheromone** ensures every path remains sampleable (Step 1).
- **Bounded deposition** combined with positive evaporation ensures the field remains bounded above, preventing pathological accumulation (necessary to keep Step 1's probability bound away from zero).
- **Positive evaporation** prevents the field from stagnating on a single path.
- **Elitist archive** is what makes the result a probability-one convergence rather than a weaker statement about iteration averages.

Removing any hypothesis breaks the proof.

## Convergence rate

The theorem is asymptotic; it does not bound the iteration count required to find $s^*$ with high probability.
Concrete rate bounds are problem-instance-dependent and typically very loose.
Empirically, ACO finds high-quality solutions to TSP-class problems in O(n) iterations for n-city instances, but this is empirical, not a consequence of the convergence theorem.

## Engineering consequences

**Choose ACO when the problem has a clear combinatorial structure with locally-evaluable solution components.** TSP, job-shop scheduling, vehicle routing, network routing — all classical ACO success cases.
Problems without local solution components (open-ended planning, text generation, dialog) do not fit the theorem's hypotheses.

**Use elitist variants for production deployments.** Non-elitist ACO has weaker convergence guarantees (convergence in iteration-average, not probability-one).
The elitist archive is a small implementation cost for a much stronger guarantee.

**Tune $\tau_{\min}$ and $\rho$ together.** Both parameters control the balance between exploration and exploitation.
The classical guidance is to set $\tau_{\min}$ as a fraction of $\tau_{\max}$ (Stützle–Hoos recommend $\tau_{\min} = \tau_{\max} / (2N)$ for $N$-component solutions) and to set $\rho \approx 0.1$–$0.5$.

**Current as of:** 26 June 2026 **Scope:** Ethnomathematics as a field of research, pedagogy, historical reconstruction, philosophy, and political/ethical critique. **Important caution:** This survey treats cultural, Indigenous, diasporic, religious, craft, ecological, navigational, computational, and material practices as knowledge systems in their own right.
It does not treat them as primitive precursors to Western academic mathematics or as decorative examples to be mined for algebra, geometry, or symmetry.

## How to read this survey

Ethnomathematics is not one thing.
It is at least four overlapping projects:

1. the study of mathematical practices embedded in cultural life;
2. the academic reconstruction, comparison, and formalization of those practices;
3. a pedagogical and decolonial movement in mathematics education;
4. a philosophical challenge to what mathematics is, who gets to define it, and how mathematical authority is institutionalized.

The field is intellectually productive because these projects do not fully coincide.
The same beadwork pattern can be read as a symmetry group, a family practice, a sacred or ceremonial form, a classroom activity, a market commodity, a political assertion of continuity, or a formal design grammar.
A strong ethnomathematical account must hold these readings together without collapsing them into one another.

---

## I. Executive summary

Ethnomathematics emerged in the late twentieth century from converging dissatisfaction with the standard Eurocentric story of mathematics.
In that story, mathematics is imagined as a universal, culture-free body of formal truths whose historical arc passes from Greece to Europe to modern abstraction, while other peoples appear only as sources of examples, intuitive techniques, or pre-scientific approximations.
Ethnomathematics contests that story.
It asks how people count, measure, locate, design, infer, classify, optimize, calculate, encode, model, compare, remember, predict, and coordinate action in specific cultural, ecological, technological, and political settings.

Ubiratan D'Ambrosio's 1985 essay, usually treated as the founding manifesto of the field, defined ethnomathematics as a research program at the border of the history of mathematics and cultural anthropology.
His formulation did not merely add non-European examples to a European curriculum.
It asked how mathematical ideas arise from culturally organized ways of explaining, knowing, surviving, and acting.
Later accounts by Marcia Ascher, Alan Bishop, Paulus Gerdes, Claudia Zaslavsky, Ron Eglash, Bill Barton, Arthur Powell, Marilyn Frankenstein, Milton Rosa, Daniel Orey, and many others expanded this program into a field spanning anthropology, mathematics education, history of science, philosophy, design, craft studies, Indigenous studies, and science and technology studies.

The field remains contested because it touches the identity of mathematics itself.
One camp treats mathematics as universal but differentially expressed: every culture may count, pattern, or measure, but the resulting practices are ultimately partial expressions of one mathematics.
A pluralist camp treats mathematics as a family of practices rather than a single object: what counts as mathematics depends on forms of life, goals, notations, technologies, proof norms, institutions, and material constraints.
Between these poles are many intermediate positions.
Some researchers want to show that Indigenous or African or Pacific or diasporic practices contain "real mathematics" such as group theory, graph theory, recursion, modular arithmetic, optimization, topology, or combinatorics.
Others warn that this defense can reproduce the very hierarchy it rejects: a practice is granted legitimacy only after being translated into academic mathematics.

The contemporary frontier is therefore not just the discovery of more examples.
It is methodological and ethical.
Researchers now ask: Who has authority to identify a practice as mathematical?
What happens when sacred, restricted, or community-governed knowledge is turned into a dataset?
Can formalization be reciprocal rather than extractive?
Can mathematics education be transformed rather than merely diversified by adding culturally themed word problems?
How do Indigenous data sovereignty, community review, refusal, and Local Contexts labels reshape mathematical research?
What would AI trained on cultural pattern archives do to living traditions?
Can communities build their own formal archives, computational design tools, or curricula without surrendering control?

Recent scholarship shows several visible trends.
First, literature reviews and bibliometric studies indicate rapid growth, especially in mathematics education and especially in Indonesia, Latin America, Africa, and Indigenous education contexts.
A 2024 scoping review by Hongzhang Xu and Rowena Ball mapped 169 studies from 1984 to 2023, identifying two broad research orientations: identifying mathematical concepts in Indigenous and traditional practices, and systematizing those concepts into more explicit frameworks.
A 2026 bibliometric analysis of 210 Scopus-indexed publications from 2010 to 2024 similarly describes an expanding but uneven field.
Second, Indigenous data governance frameworks such as CARE, OCAP, and Local Contexts have begun to change the ethical baseline: not all knowledge should be open, digitized, or formalized.
Third, the rise of AI and machine learning has created a new extraction risk.
Pattern archives, khipu databases, textile datasets, language corpora, and image repositories can be modeled computationally, but without community governance this repeats colonial collection under a technical name.

Mathematically, the field has become richer and more precise.
Khipu research now uses corpus analysis and data science to test accounting relations among hundreds of knotted-string records.
Sona and related sand-drawing traditions are studied through Eulerian graph theory, drawing algorithms, and greatest-common-divisor constructions, while researchers also emphasize that the drawings are story-bearing performance practices.
Kolam research connects ritual drawing to graph traversal, picture grammars, one-stroke generation, modular structure, and, recently, community-sensitive data physicalization.
Pacific navigation involves star compasses, swell patterns, dead reckoning, embodied spherical reasoning, and relational orientation rather than map-centered abstraction.
African fractal architecture and design involve recursion, scaling, and generative procedures, but reductive "this is just fractals" readings miss ritual, social, settlement, and aesthetic meanings.
Beadwork, weaving, basketry, and textiles open research problems in symmetry, color constraints, braid and knot structures, topology, linear algebra, tiling, and embodied fabrication.
Games such as mancala connect counting, strategy, state spaces, invariants, combinatorial game theory, and social pedagogy.
Music and dance bring modular time, Euclidean rhythms, cyclic permutations, embodied timing, and gesture-space geometry into mathematical view.

The strongest current work is neither anti-mathematical nor naïvely celebratory.
It accepts that formalization can reveal deep structure, support education, and create new mathematics.
It also insists that formalization can distort, appropriate, or desacralize.
The frontier lies in methods that can do both: mathematical modeling that is precise enough to matter to mathematicians, and accountable enough not to turn living knowledge into raw material for institutional extraction.

The next decade will likely be shaped by five pressures.
First, Indigenous and community-led scholarship will demand stronger protocols for consent, authorship, compensation, data governance, and refusal.
Second, AI will intensify the stakes of pattern extraction, language modeling, and automated classification.
Third, mathematics education will continue to fight over whether culturally sustaining and decolonial mathematics is rigorous transformation or political dilution; the answer will depend on whether curricula change epistemic authority, not merely examples.
Fourth, material mathematics—textiles, beadwork, architecture, basketry, carving, ceramics, knotting, navigation tools—will become a major interdisciplinary frontier connecting topology, mechanics, computation, and craft.
Fifth, philosophy of mathematics will have to engage ethnomathematics more seriously: not as a sociological add-on, but as evidence that mathematical objects, proofs, models, and practices are stabilized through institutions, tools, languages, bodies, and lands.

## II. Definitions and scope

## 1. D'Ambrosio and the emergence of the term

D'Ambrosio's 1985 article, "Ethnomathematics and Its Place in the History and Pedagogy of Mathematics," named a research program that sits between the history of mathematics, anthropology, and mathematics education.
Later summaries often gloss ethnomathematics as the mathematical practices of identifiable cultural groups.
D'Ambrosio also parsed the word etymologically: *ethno* as cultural environment, *mathema* as explanation/understanding/knowing, and *tics* from techniques or arts.
This etymology matters because it shifts mathematics from a noun to an activity: ways of explaining, coping, ordering, designing, and knowing.

D'Ambrosio's program also had an ethical horizon.
He repeatedly linked ethnomathematics to peace, social justice, and critique of domination.
The point was not only to recognize hidden mathematics in cultural practices, but to contest the educational and political systems that position some peoples as mathematically capable and others as deficient.

## 2. Mathematics as cultural practice

A cultural-practice definition treats mathematics as something people do.
It includes counting systems, body-based numeration, land measurement, star navigation, calendrical calculation, trade accounting, craft design, kinship classification, game strategy, ritual patterning, ecological timing, and material fabrication.
The practices may not be separated from religion, law, kinship, subsistence, aesthetics, or governance.
Indeed, the separation of "mathematics" from those domains is itself historically specific.

This definition is attractive because it does not require a practice to resemble classroom mathematics before being studied.
Its risk is overextension: if every ordered practice is mathematics, the term loses discrimination.
Good ethnomathematics therefore needs criteria: not rigid external criteria, but careful attention to counting, measuring, relational ordering, invariants, transformations, proof-like justification, optimization, algorithmic repetition, reversible operations, pattern generation, error correction, and other features that make a practice mathematically consequential without forcing it into a predetermined academic template.

## 3. Ethnomathematics as education reform

In mathematics education, ethnomathematics has been used to make curricula culturally relevant, culturally responsive, culturally sustaining, anti-racist, Indigenizing, and decolonial.
The strongest versions do more than add cultural artifacts to worksheets.
They ask whose knowledge counts, which languages can carry mathematical reasoning, which problems matter to a community, how learners' existing practices can be treated as intellectual resources, and how mathematics can be taught without requiring cultural assimilation.

The weakest versions become tokenism: a Navajo rug pattern inserted into a geometry lesson, a mancala board used to teach arithmetic, or a beadwork image used to decorate a linear algebra assignment without community context, Indigenous authority, or attention to the politics of knowledge.
Contemporary education research increasingly distinguishes representational inclusion from epistemic transformation.

## 4. Ethnomathematics as anthropology and history of knowledge

Anthropological and historical ethnomathematics asks how mathematical ideas appear in archives, artifacts, oral traditions, everyday labor, performance, craft, ritual, and social organization.
It studies how knowledge is transmitted, how procedures are validated, how practitioners identify error, how expertise is distributed, and how practices change under trade, missionization, schooling, colonization, industrialization, tourism, digital archiving, and market commodification.

This strand is close to the anthropology of number, history of science, material culture studies, cognitive anthropology, and STS.
It is also vulnerable to classic anthropological problems: outsider authority, colonial archives, translation asymmetry, informant extraction, and publication of knowledge that communities may not want public.

## 5. Ethnomathematics as decolonial critique

As decolonial critique, ethnomathematics targets the coloniality of mathematical authority.
It asks why modern institutions often treat European formal mathematics as universal reason and other practices as culture.
It asks how schools, exams, development projects, technical standards, land surveys, census categories, and economic models imposed colonial order.
It also asks how communities can reclaim or continue mathematical knowledge without simply translating it into institutional terms.

This strand is strongly shaped by Indigenous research methodologies, critical mathematics education, antiracist education, and decolonial theory.
Its key terms include sovereignty, refusal, reciprocity, community accountability, epistemic justice, and knowledge governance.

## 6. Ethnomathematics as philosophy of mathematics

Philosophically, ethnomathematics challenges familiar positions:

- **Realism/Platonism:** If mathematics is a realm of abstract objects, then cultural practices are different routes to the same truths.
  Ethnomathematics becomes history and pedagogy, not ontology.
- **Formalism:** If mathematics is formal symbol manipulation, many cultural practices are proto-formal or informal until encoded.
  Ethnomathematics becomes a source of structures for formalization.
- **Constructivism/pragmatism:** Mathematical objects are constructed through activity, proof, tools, notation, and use.
  Ethnomathematics becomes evidence that different practices construct different stable objects.
- **Pluralism:** There may be many legitimate mathematical worlds, logics, or practices, not merely many examples of one mathematics.
- **Decolonial epistemology:** The issue is not only ontology but power: who can declare an object mathematical, what institutions enforce that declaration, and what forms of life are erased when mathematics is purified from context.

## 7. Universalist and pluralist tensions

The universalist impulse says: two plus two is four everywhere; a symmetry group is a symmetry group everywhere; if a craft pattern instantiates a wallpaper group, that fact is not culturally relative.
The pluralist response says: the statement may be formally true, but the practice is not exhausted by it.
A weaver may not be "doing wallpaper groups" in the social sense, even if a mathematician can construct a wallpaper-group model from the cloth.
Conversely, a community may possess rich mathematical knowledge even where no Western theorem is immediately visible.

A mature position distinguishes **formal equivalence**, **practical equivalence**, **epistemic equivalence**, and **political equivalence**.
A model may be formally correct while practically irrelevant, epistemically distorting, or politically extractive.
The task is not to abandon formalization, but to situate it.

---

## III. Historical foundations

## 1. Colonial encounters and the classification of knowledge

Modern mathematics developed alongside colonial classification: mapping, surveying, accounting, taxation, navigation, logistics, astronomy, ballistics, census-making, and racialized schooling.
Colonial institutions frequently treated Indigenous and local mathematical practices as superstition, craft habit, or practical rule-of-thumb, while extracting land knowledge, navigational knowledge, calendrical knowledge, agricultural timing, architecture, and design.

The colonial archive is therefore both indispensable and dangerous.
It contains records of practices disrupted by colonization, but those records are filtered through missionaries, administrators, ethnographers, traders, and school officials.
Errors in transcription, mistranslation, and missing protocol context are common.
Contemporary work in Indigenous astronomy, for example, warns that early records may misidentify stars or omit cultural restrictions.
Similar caution applies to khipu, sand drawings, beadwork, ecological calendars, and kinship systems.

## 2. Anthropology of number, measure, space, time, and pattern

Long before ethnomathematics was named, anthropologists and historians studied numeration, counting gestures, body-based systems, calendrical cycles, spatial orientation, and trade calculation.
These studies often oscillated between fascination and evolutionism.
Some treated non-European systems as evidence of "primitive mentality" or cognitive limitation.
Later scholarship reversed that framing, showing that numeration and calculation are technologies embedded in practical life.
A body-counting system, for example, is not a failed place-value system; it is a culturally organized mapping between body, gesture, memory, and quantity.

## 3. History of mathematics beyond Greece and Europe

Ethnomathematics overlaps with the broader project of writing world histories of mathematics: Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, African, Mesoamerican, Andean, Pacific, Arctic, and other traditions.
The distinction is that history of mathematics often focuses on texts, proofs, astronomies, algorithms, and institutions that can be placed in a global academic genealogy.
Ethnomathematics more readily includes craft, oral knowledge, embodied practice, local computation, and living tradition.
The two fields are complementary when both avoid civilizational ranking.

## 4. Foundational figures

### Ubiratan D'Ambrosio D'Ambrosio gave the field its name and its political ambition.
His work connected mathematics education, cultural history, and critique of domination.
He treated mathematics not as a neutral universal possession but as a set of techniques for knowing and acting that are historically and culturally located.

### Marcia Ascher Ascher's *Ethnomathematics: A Multicultural View of Mathematical Ideas* (1991) remains one of the clearest mathematical introductions.
Her examples include kinship systems, khipu, games, graph-like drawings, and mathematical ideas outside written proof traditions.
Her strength is mathematical clarity; the limitation, from a contemporary view, is that the field now demands deeper community governance and sovereignty analysis than early synthetic work usually provided.

### Alan Bishop Bishop's influential account identified six mathematical activities widely found across cultures: counting, locating, measuring, designing, playing, and explaining.
This taxonomy helped educators see mathematics as activity rather than only curriculum content.
Its limitation is that a universal activity list can still impose an external frame if not handled carefully.

### Claudia Zaslavsky Zaslavsky's *Africa Counts* (1973; later editions) documented number, pattern, games, music, architecture, and other mathematical practices across sub-Saharan Africa.
It was foundational for both African mathematics history and multicultural mathematics education.
It also represents an early effort to challenge the absence of African intellectual traditions from school mathematics.

### Paulus Gerdes Gerdes developed some of the most mathematically detailed work in ethnomathematics, especially on African geometry, sona drawings, basketry, mat weaving, and design.
His work often reconstructs geometric reasoning from craft procedures and shows how it can generate mathematical problems.
Contemporary readers should pair his formal reconstructions with community-centered and anti-extractive protocols.

### Ron Eglash Eglash's *African Fractals* (1999) brought recursion, scaling, and computational design into public view.
It showed fractal-like organization in architecture, settlement layout, hairstyling, textiles, sculpture, and symbolic systems.
Its importance is enormous, but the slogan "African fractals" can become reductive when detached from local meanings and practices.

### Gloria Ford Gilmer and ISGEm Gloria Ford Gilmer was a major organizer of ethnomathematics in the United States and a co-founder of the International Study Group on Ethnomathematics in 1985.
ISGEm helped institutionalize the field through networks, conferences, and publications connecting mathematics, culture, social justice, and decolonization.

### Bill Barton, Arthur Powell, Marilyn Frankenstein, Milton Rosa, Daniel Orey, and others These scholars expanded ethnomathematics in mathematics education, critical pedagogy, curriculum design, teacher education, and theoretical clarification.
Barton sharpened definitional issues; Powell and Frankenstein connected mathematics education to democracy and social justice; Rosa and Orey developed curricula, modeling frameworks, and global syntheses.

## 5. Practices historically studied

Ethnomathematics has studied mathematical reasoning in:

- craft: weaving, basketry, beadwork, carving, ceramics, textiles, knotting;
- architecture: settlement plans, house forms, sacred buildings, Islamic geometric patterns;
- navigation: star paths, swell reading, wayfinding, orientation systems;
- music and dance: rhythm cycles, modular timing, floor patterns, gesture sequences;
- games: mancala, strategy games, puzzles, race games, gambling and probability;
- agriculture and ecology: seasonal calendars, phenology, irrigation, land division;
- astronomy and calendars: lunar/solar cycles, ritual calendars, star knowledge;
- trade and accounting: numeration, tallying, khipu, weights, measures, exchange;
- language and kinship: classifiers, relation systems, taxonomies, spatial deixis.

## 6. Nation-states, colonial schools, and mathematics education

Colonial and national schooling often used mathematics to rank populations and train bureaucratic subjects.
Standard curricula displaced local knowledge by treating school mathematics as the only real mathematics.
Ethnomathematics entered teacher education partly as a repair: it sought to reconnect students' lived knowledge with formal learning.
The danger is that schools can absorb ethnomathematics as multicultural decoration while preserving the hierarchy that caused the harm.
The frontier is therefore not inclusion alone but authority: who designs the curriculum, who benefits, who reviews it, and what knowledge remains outside the classroom by community choice.
